subject: Pathology
summary: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a DNA virus that infects epithelial cells, causing warts and, for high‑risk types, precancerous lesions that can progress to cancer. Persistent infection of the cervical transformation zone is the key step in oncogenesis.

sections.p: HPV is a small, non‑enveloped double‑stranded DNA virus that infects basal epithelial cells after micro‑abrasion. Low‑risk types (6, 11) cause benign warts; high‑risk types (16, 18, 45, 31, 33, 52, 58) can lead to dysplasia and cancer.
HPV capsid proteins L1 and L2 form the outer shell; early proteins (E1‑E7) drive replication and oncogenesis. E6 degrades p53; E7 inactivates Rb, allowing uncontrolled cell division.
b: Low‑risk types lack strong oncogenic activity

sections.p: Virus enters through micro‑abrasions, reaches basal layer, replicates as cells differentiate, and is shed in skin or mucosal secretions. Latent infection can persist for years.
b: Perinatal transmission can cause respiratory papillomatosis
Fomite spread possible but less common

sections.p: Low‑risk HPV produces condylomata acuminata (genital warts). High‑risk HPV causes cervical intra‑epithelial neoplasia (CIN) that can progress to invasive cervical cancer; also anal, penile, vulvar, vaginal, and oropharyngeal cancers.
b: High‑risk HPV infection is necessary but not sufficient for cancer

sections.p: Screening combines cytology (Pap smear) and HPV DNA testing. Histology confirms CIN grade. In low‑resource settings, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) is used.

t.b: Detects abnormal squamous cells; ASC-US or higher prompts HPV testing or colposcopy
Identifies presence of oncogenic types; positive with normal cytology indicates need for surveillance
Provides definitive histologic grade; guides treatment
Detects acetowhite lesions in settings without cytology; positive result leads to cryotherapy or referral

sections.p: Management targets the lesion and prevents progression. Low‑risk warts are treated locally; high‑risk precancers are excised or ablated. Vaccination prevents infection.
b: Cryotherapy or topical imiquimod for genital warts
HPV vaccine (bivalent, quadrivalent, nonavalent) given before sexual debut

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams.
b: High‑risk HPV types 16/18 cause ~70% of cervical cancers
E6/E7 oncoproteins inactivate p53 and Rb
Screening: Pap + HPV co‑test every 5 years after 30 y

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent genital warts, especially large or bleeding
Abnormal Pap smear or positive high‑risk HPV test
Unexplained pelvic pain, bleeding, or mass

faq.q: Can HPV infection be cleared without treatment?
faq.a: Yes, most low‑risk infections clear spontaneously; high‑risk infections may persist and need monitoring.

faq.q: Is the HPV vaccine useful after infection?
faq.a: Vaccination protects against types not yet acquired and is still recommended even after prior infection.

faq.q: Why are HIV‑positive patients at higher risk for HPV‑related cancer?
faq.a: Immunosuppression reduces clearance of high‑risk HPV, increasing persistence and progression.
